lines: Let $\EE$ be an [[Definition:Experiment|experiment]] with [[Definition:Probability Space|probability space]] $\struct {\Omega, \Sigma, \Pr}$.
Let $A, B \in \Sigma$ be [[Definition:Event|events]] of $\EE$ such that $\map \Pr B > 0$.
The '''[[Definition:Conditional Probability|conditional probability of $A$ given $B$]]''' is:
Suppose it is given that $B$ has [[Definition:Occurrence of Event|occurred]].
Then the [[Definition:Probability|probability]] of $A$ having [[Definition:Occurrence of Event|occurred]] may not be $\map \Pr A$ after all.
In fact, we ''can'' say that $A$ has [[Definition:Occurrence of Event|occurred]] {{iff}} $A \cap B$ has [[Definition:Occurrence of Event|occurred]].
So, if we ''know'' that $B$ has [[Definition:Occurrence of Event|occurred]], the [[Definition:Conditional Probability|conditional probability]] of $A$ given $B$ is $\map \Pr {A \cap B}$.
:if we ''don't'' actually know whether $B$ has [[Definition:Occurrence of Event|occurred]] or not

:The [[Definition:Probability|probability]] that $A$ and $B$ have both [[Definition:Occurrence of Event|occurred]] is the [[Definition:Conditional Probability|conditional probability]] of $A$ given $B$ [[Definition:Real Multiplication|multiplied]] by the [[Definition:Probability|probability]] that $B$ has [[Definition:Occurrence of Event|occurred]].
